title: The One Nobody Heard — Violation, Deceit, the Sword
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. This chapter is a hard one to preach, and before we begin I want to ask you to let your heart go soft. Because what we are about to read is one of the darkest chapters in the whole Bible; and I know that here in this room, and online, there will certainly be someone carrying the very wound this chapter describes.

So let me say one thing first, and I want you to hear it clearly: the one who was hurt did nothing wrong. From the first verse of this chapter to the last, God does not rebuke Dinah with a single word, and the narrator does not rebuke her with a single word. If anyone has ever used Scripture to hint to you, "If you hadn't gone out, none of this would have happened" — that is not what the Bible says. That is something people added.

Let me start with a question. In a family, what happens when the person who was hurt most says nothing at all, from beginning to end? Genesis 34 runs to thirty-one verses, and Dinah is not given one line. Her father hears about it and holds his peace. Her brothers burn with anger, and then they take swords and slaughter a whole city. And the first full sentence the father speaks about the matter is this: "You have troubled me."
1. She Went Out, and for Thirty-One Verses She Never Says a Word
"Dinah, the daughter of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob, went out to see the daughters of the land." (Genesis 34:1)

"Went out" in the original is וַתֵּצֵא (*vatetse*), about as ordinary a verb as Hebrew has. She went to see the daughters of the land — she wanted friends. The text passes no comment whatever on this, not one word of blame.

But the real address of this chapter is written at the end of the previous one: Jacob "came in peace to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan … and encamped before the city." God had told him to go up to Bethel; he stopped at Shechem. And he did not merely stop — he pitched his tents right up against the city wall.

Brothers and sisters, please do not misunderstand me. I am not saying that because the father stopped in the wrong place, the daughter has to carry the blame — absolutely not. The guilt lies one hundred per cent with the man who committed the violence. What I am saying is this: when parents make a spiritual decision, the price is very often not paid by the parents. That is the first heartbreaking thing in this chapter.
Verse 2: "Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the land, saw her. He took her, lay with her, and humbled her."

"He took her" is וַיִּקַּח (*vayiqach*) — that verb "to take" which keeps coming back through Genesis: Eve took the fruit, Abram took Sarai; this time what is taken is a person. "Humbled her" is וַיְעַנֶּהָ, the intensive Piel stem, literally "he made her suffer, he brought her low" — the same root as the "affliction" (עֳנִי) of Israel in Egypt.
The text speaks the language of a victim, not the language of romance. It does not call this thing "a relationship". It calls it making her suffer.

Verse 3 is a strange one: "His soul joined to Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, and he loved the young lady, and spoke kindly to the young lady." Behind "his soul joined" is וַתִּדְבַּק נַפְשׁוֹ, literally "his soul stuck fast" — and that is the very word of Genesis 2, where a man will "join with his wife."

This is the verse in the whole chapter that calls for the most watchfulness. A man who has committed violence can say the tenderest things afterwards; he may even genuinely believe that what he feels is love. "Spoke kindly to the young lady" is, in the Hebrew, "he spoke to her heart." Brothers and sisters, sweet words after the harm do not turn the harm into love. What you must look at is not what he said afterwards. It is what he did at the time.
Then verse 5: "Now Jacob heard that he had defiled Dinah, his daughter … Jacob held his peace until they came."
"Held his peace" is וְהֶחֱרִשׁ, a Hiphil, the causative stem — literally "he made himself keep silent." That is not a man who had no time to react. That is a choice.

Someone will ask: isn't silence a spiritual virtue? Brothers and sisters, not to be angry when anger is what the moment calls for is not maturity; it is dereliction of duty. Ephesians says, "Be angry, and don't sin" — Scripture nowhere forbids righteous anger. What Scripture forbids is the sin inside the anger. A father who holds his peace while his daughter is being defiled is not being gentle. He is absent.

And notice the second half of verse 5: "until they came." He is waiting for his sons to come home and deal with it. A father takes the thing he himself ought to have carried and drops it down onto his sons; and so the matter lands in the hands of a few hot-blooded young men. A great many family tragedies begin exactly like this — not because somebody did something wrong, but because somebody did not do what he should have done.

Verses 6 and 7 hold a contrast that stings as you read it. Hamor comes out to talk business with Jacob, while Jacob's sons only hear of it when they "came in from the field"; and the moment they hear, they are "grieved", and they are "very angry". "Grieved" in the original is וַיִּתְעַצְּבוּ, the same verb used in Genesis 6, when God looked at the wickedness of humanity and "it grieved him in his heart". And "very angry" is, literally, "it burned in them". The brothers' reaction was right. What they did next was wrong. Those two things have to be preached separately.
Some people say Dinah's "going out" is what brought this on. Is that a right reading?

It is completely wrong, and reading it that way does real damage. The verb "went out" in verse 1 is about as ordinary a verb as Hebrew has; the text passes no comment on what she did, and God does not rebuke her with a single word. In the whole chapter there is exactly one person the text holds responsible, and that is the man who committed the violence. Reading "she went out" as the cause of it is something later readers added; it is not what the Bible says. This matters enormously, because a person who hears that said in church is wounded a second time. So for anyone teaching this chapter there is only one test: when someone who has been hurt in this way has heard you out, will they come away feeling that it was their own fault? If so, you have taught it wrongly.
The father "held his peace". Isn't that patience?

The Hebrew is a causative stem, literally "he made himself keep silent" — that is not a man who had no time to react, it is a choice. And the second half of the verse matters even more: "until they came." He is waiting for his sons to come home and handle it. Ephesians says, "Be angry, and don't sin"; Scripture does not forbid righteous anger, it forbids the sin inside the anger. So failing to be angry when anger is what the moment calls for is not maturity, it is dereliction of duty. This chapter carries a heavy reminder for parents and for leaders: the tragedy in a household very often comes not because somebody did something wrong, but because somebody did not do what he should have done — and then the matter lands in the hands of a few hot-blooded young men.
2. A Light from the Original: Which Side the Text Itself Is On

Some people read this chapter and ask: what does the Bible actually make of what happened here? The text answers that question very clearly indeed — the answer is simply tucked away inside a few words.
Verse 7: "The men were grieved, and they were very angry, because he had done folly in Israel in lying with Jacob's daughter, a thing that ought not to be done."

"Folly" in the original is נְבָלָה (*nevalah*). This is the heaviest word the Old Testament has for sexual violence; Deuteronomy 22 uses it, and so does Judges 19. It does not mean "an indiscretion". It means a vile and degrading outrage.

"A thing that ought not to be done" — וְכֵן לֹא יֵעָשֶׂה. That line is not spoken by any character in the story. It is a verdict the narrator himself breaks in to deliver. In the whole book of Genesis there are very few places where the narrator passes judgement as directly as this.
In other words, the Bible does not leave this hanging in some grey area. God's own word has said it out loud: this was an outrage, and it ought not to have been done.

And there is one more detail. Verse 7 is the first time this family is spoken of as Israel — the phrase is בְיִשְׂרָאֵל, "in Israel". The new name Jacob had only just been given back in chapter 32 becomes, for the first time, the name of a whole people — and the first time it appears, it appears inside a sentence saying that a thing like this must not happen in Israel.
Brothers and sisters, at the very moment the people of God are given their name, Scripture lays down a boundary first: a thing like this may not happen among the people of God.

So if you are the one who was hurt, I want you to hear where God stands. He did not stay silent — he said, "this is folly, an outrage." He did not rebuke you; the one he rebuked was the man who committed the violence. You do not have to carry the responsibility for somebody else's sin.

And let me say something practical as well: a wound like this is not healed by one sermon. If you are carrying a wound like this, please go to a pastor you trust, or a counsellor, or a qualified professional helper, and let that wound be properly heard by somebody, once. Scripture says, "Weep with those who weep" — the church was always meant to be a place where a person is allowed to cry.
After the violence he "spoke kindly to her". Doesn't that show that he really did love her?

The word "joined" in verse 3 is literally "his soul stuck fast", and "spoke kindly" is, in the Hebrew, "he spoke to her heart" — the text writes it very tenderly indeed, and that is precisely why this verse is the place in the chapter that calls for the most watchfulness. A man who has committed violence can say the tenderest things afterwards, and he may even genuinely believe that what he feels is love. But sweet words after the harm do not turn the harm into love. The principle for telling the difference is simple: look not at what he said afterwards but at what he did at the time — and at whether he has admitted that it was wrong, and whether he has borne the consequences. That test applies just as well to relationships today.
Has the Bible itself taken a position on what happened here?

It has, and very clearly. The word rendered "folly" in verse 7 is נְבָלָה in the original, the heaviest word the Old Testament has for sexual violence. And the line "a thing that ought not to be done" is not spoken by any character in the story; it is a verdict the narrator himself breaks in to deliver — and in the whole book of Genesis there are very few places where he passes judgement as directly as that. There is one further detail: this verse is the first time the family is called "Israel". At the very moment the people of God are given their name, Scripture lays down a boundary first: a thing like this may not happen among the people of God. So if you are carrying a wound like this, hear where God stands: he did not stay silent.
3. Taking the Sign of the Covenant and Using It as a Weapon
Hamor and Shechem come to ask for the girl, and the terms they offer are generous: intermarriage between the families, living together in the land, trading in it, acquiring property in it.

"Get possessions in it" is built on אֲחֻזָּה, the technical term for a holding in the promised land. What the city of Shechem is offering is a counterfeit of the very things God had promised — land, property, peace, prosperity. The devil never tempts anybody with something ugly. He uses the things God has already promised, only reached through the wrong door.
Then verse 13: "The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and Hamor his father with deceit when they spoke, because he had defiled Dinah their sister."
"With deceit" is בְּמִרְמָה (*bemirmah*). In Genesis 27, when Isaac discovers the truth, he says, "Your brother came with deceit, and has taken away your blessing." The same word.

Brothers and sisters, this is the family weapon, handed down. The father used deceit to take a blessing; the sons use deceit to butcher a city. Sin that is never dealt with does not stop at your generation. It changes into a bigger shape and shows up in your children.

And the weapon they choose is circumcision. In Genesis 17 God gives Abraham the sign of the covenant: "Every male among you shall be circumcised … It will be a token of the covenant between me and you." That is the seal of grace, the warrant of an identity.
They used it as an anaesthetic. Verse 25: "On the third day, when they were sore, two of Jacob's sons … each took his sword, came upon the unsuspecting city, and killed all the males."

"On the third day" — the day after surgery when the pain is at its worst and a man is least able to defend himself. "Unsuspecting" is בֶּטַח in the original, literally "in a sense of safety". They picked out the exact moment when people trusted them most, and struck.

Brothers and sisters, this is the most terrible thing in the whole chapter. Not the sword — the sign. To take something holy and use it as a weapon is more terrible than open violence, because it borrows the name of God.

We do not use swords today, but we do use Scripture. "You are to submit." "You are to forgive." "You are not to judge." The same words can be medicine and the same words can be a blade. The difference lies here: are you trying to help this person, or are you trying to shut him up?

And let me add this in passing: why did the whole city of Shechem agree to it? In verse 23 Hamor's son tells them the truth: "Won't their livestock and their possessions and all their animals be ours?" They were not persuaded by love. They were persuaded by profit. Both sides were calculating — and a whole city paid for it with their lives.
Why is their use of circumcision as a weapon more terrible than the sword itself?

Because circumcision is the sign of the covenant God gave Abraham in Genesis 17 — the seal of grace, the warrant of an identity. They turned it into an anaesthetic. "On the third day, when they were sore": that is the day after surgery when the pain is at its worst and a man is least able to defend himself; and "unsuspecting" is, in the original, literally "in a sense of safety". They picked out the exact moment when people trusted them most, and struck. To take something holy and use it as a weapon is more terrible than open violence, because it borrows the name of God. We do not use swords today, but we do use Scripture: "you are to submit", "you are to forgive" — the same words can be medicine and the same words can be a blade.
4. "You Have Troubled Me" — the Father's First Thought
After the slaughter of the city, Jacob finally opens his mouth. In this whole chapter, this is the first complete sentence he speaks about what has happened:

"You have troubled me, to make me odious to the inhabitants of the land, among the Canaanites and the Perizzites. I am few in number. They will gather themselves together against me and strike me, and I will be destroyed, I and my house." (Genesis 34:30)
Count how many times "me" and "I" turn up in that one sentence. You have troubled me; you have made me odious; I am few in number; they will strike me; I will be destroyed, I and my house.
His daughter has been violated, a whole city lies dead, the women and the little ones have been carried off — and the father's first thought is still: what does this do to me?

Brothers and sisters, this is the self-centred life. The self-centred life is not a matter of having done something wicked. The self-centred life is this: whatever happens, my first thought is myself. It can look perfectly respectable, it can sound perfectly reasonable, it can even be phrased in very spiritual language — but the focus is on me.

"You have troubled" is עֲכַרְתֶּם in the original. In Joshua 7, when Achan is found out, Joshua says to him, "Why have you troubled us?" — the same word, and Achan goes down in Israel's memory as the man who troubled Israel. Jacob hangs that label on his sons, and what he says is not even untrue; but not once has he asked the one question: how is Dinah?
The last verse of the chapter is a question flung back at him by his sons: "Should he deal with our sister as with a prostitute?" (Genesis 34:31)
Nobody answers. The text simply stops there.

The last word in the Hebrew is אֲחוֹתֵנוּ — "our sister". In the whole chapter, the one word that treats Dinah as a person, as somebody's own flesh and blood, falls in the very last word. And the men who say it have just butchered a city.

The bill for all this is not settled for another forty years. In Genesis 49, blessing his sons on his deathbed, Jacob says of Simeon and Levi, "Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel." What a household leaves unaddressed is always carried over and settled in the next generation.
Why is Jacob's "You have troubled me" the most stinging line in the chapter?

Count how many times "me" and "I" turn up in that one sentence: you have troubled me; you have made me odious; I am few in number; they will strike me; I will be destroyed, I and my house. His daughter has been violated, a whole city lies dead, the women and the little ones have been carried off — and the father's first thought is still what this does to him. That is exactly what the self-centred life looks like. The self-centred life is not a matter of having done something wicked; the self-centred life is that whatever happens, my first thought is myself. It can look perfectly respectable, it can sound perfectly reasonable, it can even be phrased in very spiritual language. And from the beginning of the chapter to the end he never once asks: how is Dinah? The practice of selflessness begins at the moment a person is able to ask that question.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
This chapter is far too easy to preach out of shape, and there are several places we must all be able to recognise.

The first distortion is hinting that Dinah's "going out" is the cause of what happened. The text has not one word of blame for her; the guilt lies wholly with the man who committed the violence. Preached the other way, it makes brothers and sisters who have been hurt suffer a second wound inside the church. The test is this: when someone who has been hurt in this way has heard you out, will they come away feeling that it was their own fault?

The second distortion is preaching Simeon and Levi's slaughter of the city as a model of righteous anger. In Genesis 49, on his deathbed, Jacob says with his own mouth that their anger was fierce and cursed; the text's assessment could hardly be clearer. Preach it as a model and what the congregation learns is not justice — it is permission to dress revenge up as justice.

The third distortion is talking only about what the sons got wrong and never about the father's silence. "He held his peace" in verse 5 and "you have troubled me" in verse 30 are where the real disease of this chapter lies. Skip them, and all the sermon has left is a telling-off for young men. When the parents in the room have heard you out, has any light fallen on them?

The fourth distortion is using the fate of Shechem to imply that some group of people ought to be wiped out. This is narrative, not command; and the text's verdict on this massacre is a negative one. Any use of this chapter to make hatred respectable is a misuse, and it is to be refused on the spot.

The fifth distortion is rushing a wounded person to "hurry up and forgive". Forgiveness is God's command, and it is the road out in the end; but it is not a painkiller, and still less is it an instrument for shutting someone up. The order runs like this: first to be heard, then to be believed, then to be protected — and only then to move towards forgiveness. Forgiveness that skips those first three steps is usually nothing but one more silence.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: our culture is deeply afraid of family shame becoming public. When something happens, the first reaction is very often "don't let this get out" — for the sake of face, for the sake of the family name, for the sake of the church's image. That is exactly what Jacob is saying: "to make me odious to the inhabitants of the land." Brothers and sisters, covering a thing over is not protection. Covering a thing over buries the person who was hurt a second time. The household of God is not held together by concealment; it is held together by light. First John says, "But if we walk in the light as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another." What ought to be reported must be reported, what ought to be dealt with must be dealt with, and what ought to be apologised for must be apologised for.

The second question: we are used to handling conflict by silence. Something happens in the family, the adults say nothing, and so the children interpret it for themselves and then go and settle it for themselves — usually by the most extreme means available. Simeon and Levi's swords were sharpened in their father's silence. Parents, elders, pastors, you need to know this: when you say nothing, the child does not conclude that everything is fine. The child concludes that nobody is going to protect him. This week, if there is something hanging unspoken in your house, you be the one to open your mouth.
When something like this happens in a church, how should it actually be handled so that nobody is wounded a second time?

There are several principles to settle in advance. First, believe first and listen first: do not rush to press for details, and do not open with "why were you there in the first place?" Second, safety comes first: where a crime is involved, what ought to be reported to the police must be reported to the police and what ought to be reported to the authorities must be reported; the church is not a court of law, and it may not use "family shame must not be aired" to push the matter down out of sight. Third, do not pressure the victim to forgive: forgiveness is a long road, not the homework of a single meeting, and least of all an instrument for getting the matter over with quickly. Fourth, refer on to professionals: alongside walking with the person, help them find a qualified counsellor or medical help. Fifth, dealing with the offender calls for real boundaries and real accountability, not merely one sentence of repentance.
7. Living 321 Out — Handing the Right to Judge Back to God
Brothers and sisters, let us take this lesson and tie it back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. Dinah has no voice in this entire chapter. And in the Gospels there is a woman who had bled for twelve years, who came up behind the Lord Jesus and touched his clothes, and then meant to slip quietly away. The Lord stopped. He turned round in the crowd and asked, "Who touched my clothes?" — and then he listened while she "told him all the truth". He could perfectly well have healed her and left it at that. Instead he stopped, and let a person with no voice finish saying what she had to say. That is my role model: he stops walking, so that someone who has been hurt can speak.

The Bible is my standard. The standard is not "we don't bring that up"; the standard is "a thing that ought not to be done". God's word has already passed its verdict on violence of this kind, and we do not need to go looking anywhere else for a position to hold. And in the same way the standard also says, "Don't seek revenge yourselves" — both sentences must be heard, and you may not pick out only one of them.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. In a matter like this it is very easy either to charge straight in or to shrink away from it for a lifetime. When to speak, whom to speak to, how far to take it — all of that needs guidance. Rely on the brain and lean on yourself and you end up in worry; rely on the heart and lean on the Holy Spirit and you end up in gladness. Simeon and Levi never enquired of God. They simply burned.

Let Jesus be King. "Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord." Revenge is, at bottom, the seizing of God's seat — and whoever seizes that seat always loses control of himself. These men set out to rescue their sister, and they ended by slaughtering a city. To let Jesus be King is to hand the right to judge back to him. That is not refusing to pursue the matter; it is handing the pursuit over to the one Judge who will never show favour to anybody.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. What Jacob cared about was his reputation — his own reputation. A person who gives all the glory to God no longer has to use his daughter's silence to protect his own image. You do not have to keep holding it up any longer. That glory was never yours to begin with.

Establish God's system. This chapter lets us watch a system going bad: the father stops at Shechem, the father says nothing, the sons resort to deceit, and the bill is not settled for forty years. To establish God's system is to deal with the thing in this generation — and not leave it to the children.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Silence
We come to this chapter carrying four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "That sort of thing doesn't happen in our family." Jacob thought that too. The widest breach pride ever opens is the feeling that you have no need to take precautions. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, imagining that we have it all covered; humility is returning to our originally intended position as human beings and admitting that I need boundaries, I need companions, and I need people who will warn me.

The fearful heart says, "If I say it out loud, won't it only get worse?" I understand that fear. But brothers and sisters, a thing that is never said does not disappear; it only moves somewhere else — it turns into a sword in a son's hand, it turns into a daughter's lifelong silence. Fear wants you to keep your mouth shut. The Holy Spirit wants you to find one safe person and finish saying it.

The ashamed heart says, "That thing that happened — was some of it my fault too?" Let me say it once more: the one who was hurt did nothing wrong. God settled it in verse 7 and left no room for argument — it was folly, an outrage, a thing that ought not to be done. What shame is best at is moving somebody else's sin onto your shoulders. The first thing the gospel does is to lift that load off you.

The wounded heart says, "It was all so long ago — who still cares?" The One who cares has been there the whole time. He never left the scene; he saw it; and he said in his own voice that this ought not to have been done. And he himself was once dragged out, and stripped, and watched in silence by a crowd — the One on the cross knows that place from the inside.
Four kinds of heart, and one and the same silence. And in the gospel, that silence is finally heard.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, towards God. Pray out loud to God about one wound in your family that has never been dealt with. It does not have to be said beautifully. Just say its name.
Second, towards yourself. Run a check: when bad news arrives, what is your first thought? If that first thought is always "what does this do to me?", write it down and carry it to the Lord.

Third, towards people. This week, find one person who is hurting and listen until he has finished. No advice, no rushing in to comfort, no spiritual language used to press him down. Simply not interrupting is already service.
Fourth, towards your daily living. This week, do not use a verse of Scripture to stop anybody's mouth. Truth is given to hold people up, not to hold people down.

Fifth, towards your mission. If you have ever used Scripture or prayer to press somebody down, go to him and apologise. This step is a hard one, but this step can pull down a wall that stands between someone and God.

Sixth, tell it to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a chapter in the Bible where a girl is violated, and she is not given one line in the whole account. Second: in that chapter God says with his own mouth that this ought not to have been done, and that the fault is not hers. Third: so the God I believe in is a God who stands on the side of the one who was hurt.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will no longer handle by silence the things that call for speech; where someone must be protected, I will stand up and protect them.
I declare that I will no longer take the holy word of God and use it as a weapon to press people down.
I declare that I hand the right to judge back to God; vengeance belongs to him, and I will not seize his seat.
I declare that whatever my family has left unaddressed, I will deal with in my own generation, and I will not leave it to my children.
I am carrying the very wound this chapter describes. What can I do this week?

Let me say the most important thing first: it was not your fault, and God has never once rebuked you. There are three very small things you can do this week. First, tell one safe person, once — you do not have to give details; "there is something very painful in my past" is enough. Being heard matters more than telling it completely. Second, find professional help: a wound like this is not healed by one sermon, so please go to a qualified counsellor or to psychiatric or psychological care. That is not unspiritual; that is taking care of yourself. Third, allow yourself to go slowly, and do not force yourself to forgive right now. God weeps with those who weep, and the church was always meant to be a place where a person is allowed to cry.
There is not one hero in this chapter. The father is silent, the sons butcher a city, a whole town is talked round by profit — and the one person who most needed to be heard does not say a word.

Why would the Bible keep a chapter like this? Because it is honest. It lets us see that a household can worship God, can build an altar, can be called Israel, and be rotting inside all the while. And God did not walk out on that household because of it.

So the focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on other people, not on the circumstances. Not I, but Christ. If this family could be repaired afterwards, it was not because a good father or a good brother finally emerged; it was because God kept on leading them towards Bethel. And if we can be healed today, it is not because we are strong enough. It is because there is One who was willing to be violated himself, to be silenced himself, to be nailed to a cross himself, so that our wounds would have somewhere to be laid down.

May God bless every one of us to become the person who is willing to stop walking and hear a wounded person all the way to the end. May our homes no longer be held together by covering things over, but held together by light. And may every cry that was never heard be heard in his presence. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.

A special reminder for this lesson: this chapter touches on sexual violence. Before you begin, say three things out loud — the one who was hurt did nothing wrong; nobody is required to tell their own story; and anyone may listen without speaking, at any point. Do not press for details, do not ask anyone to forgive, go to people yourself after the meeting, and have ready the information for local professional help you can refer people on to.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson home until it is a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ "A thing that ought not to be done" is a verdict the narrator himself breaks in to deliver. The Bible refuses to leave this in a grey area — what does that say to someone who has been hurt?
2. ★★ Sweet words after the harm do not turn the harm into love. How do you use that test in relationships today?
3. ★ The father "held his peace", and then waited "until they came". Why is failing to be angry when anger is called for not maturity?
4. ★★ They turned circumcision into a weapon. What sayings that use Scripture as a blade have you heard — or said yourself?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (that sort of thing doesn't happen in our family), fearful (saying it out loud would destroy this family), ashamed (I always thought it was my own fault), wounded (nobody has ever asked me how I am). Which are you most like? You may name the kind only; you do not have to say why.
6. ★★ Read aloud: "a thing that ought not to be done." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ In your family, or in the group you belong to, is there something everybody knows about and nobody talks about? What is it that keeps people from speaking?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "There is one thing I have always wanted to hear somebody say to me …"
9. ★★ This week, which one person will you go and ask, "How are you doing?" — and actually hear the answer all the way to the end? Say the name.

Leader's reminder: this section carries the highest risk of all. Do not press for details, do not let group members pass comment on one another, and never say "it is all over now." If someone breaks down in the group, stop at once and stay with him; go to him privately after the meeting and help him find professional support where that is needed. Where a crime is involved, or where a minor has been harmed, help make the report the law where you are requires.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your family, who is the one with no lines — the one nobody asked when it all happened? How will you ask him this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work, or in your service, whose grievance keeps being treated as unimportant?
12. ★★★ The practice of selflessness: this week, when something happens, ask "how is he doing?" first, and only then think "what does this do to me?" Name the occasion you expect to meet soon.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and ask him to say a word to you this week whenever you are rushing to reach a verdict about somebody. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a chapter in the Bible about a young woman who is violated, and across all thirty-one verses she never says a word. Second: the Bible itself breaks in with one line — "a thing that ought not to be done" — and from beginning to end it never once blames her. Third: so the God I believe in stands on the side of the one who was hurt. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other just one thing: the person you are going to ask "How are you doing?" this week. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to make our homes and our churches places where a wounded person can speak and can weep, and asking the Lord himself to comfort every brother and sister here today who is carrying a wound of this kind.
